On every simulation step it turns the commanded velocity into wheel velocities, and the Physics system moves the robot. You pass if you had the two transports, the bridge in the middle, and a system inside Gazebo that acts on the command. Missing the bridge is a partial pass, and more than that is a fail.

Gazebo describes a scene in a world file: physics settings, ground and lights, and a list of models. A model is built from links, rigid bodies with mass, inertia and both a collision and a visual shape, connected by joints. Everything a model does comes from systems, plugins the world or the model loads by name, such as one that moves every body according to physics and one that turns a wheeled robot's commanded velocity into wheel motion.

The problem is that Gazebo and ROS speak different languages entirely: ROS messages travel over DDS, and Gazebo has its own transport and its own message types, so a ROS node's publisher has nobody inside the simulator to talk to directly. A simulator also has to give every loaded system a fixed, repeatable place in each step, or a command applied after the physics has already run that step would arrive one step late, silently.

A separate bridge process subscribes to a ROS topic and republishes each message on a matching Gazebo topic, converting the type as it goes; inside the simulator, the system responsible for that behaviour is the one that actually subscribes to it. Every step runs the same sequence for every loaded system: a setup call once when the system is loaded, then, on each step, one phase that applies incoming commands, one that advances the physics, and one that publishes results such as odometry, in that fixed order every time.

The mistake under pressure is a silent one: everything starts, and nothing moves, because the bridge was given a topic name, a ROS type or a Gazebo type that doesn't match what either side actually uses, and nothing on either side reports an error, since as far as each is concerned it is talking correctly to whatever it was told to talk to. The same silence follows a model resource Gazebo can't find: the log says so, but the simulation keeps running as if the model were missing rather than broken.

You meet exactly this in the interview question itself: naming the two transports, the bridge process that sits between them, and the system inside Gazebo that turns a velocity command into a moving robot.

It takes about 5 seconds of stepping, plus a second or two to load the world and its plugins. The world asks for a real-time factor of 1 with 1 ms steps, and running without a GUI doesn't change that: 5000 steps of 1 ms are 5 s of simulated time, which Gazebo spreads over 5 s of wall-clock time. Headless saves the rendering cost, and the topic on simulation time shows how to run faster than real time.
